newsitem.title: USA: Spring gasoline price rises seen muted this year.
newsitem.headline: Spring gasoline price rises seen muted this year.

text.p: Drivers may feel less pinched at the pump this summer as a sharp drop in oil prices has already put the brakes on the seasonal upturn in gasoline prices.

"I don't expect this year's gasoline rally to show up on the front page of the newspaper," according to Tim Evans, an analyst with Pegasus Econometric Group in New York, who reckons that gasoline prices may not explode as much as they did in 1996.

Gasoline futures on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) typically rally in the beginning of spring, anticipating traditional strong demand during the summer driving season, which is the period of heaviest consumption.
Last year, gasoline futures prices rocketed 14 cents a gallon in the first month of spring alone to a post-Gulf War high of 78.10 cents on supply concerns.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) said that from April to May 1996 the national average price for a gallon of gasoline at self-serve pumps rose 14 cents to $1.31. Retail prices are now at about $1.29, but that does not yet reflect the latest declines in spot and futures markets.
Those declines will likely take several weeks to filter through to the retail pumps.

With spring just a month away, the gasoline market has turned bearish due to slack demand for heating oil. The price of crude oil on the NYMEX has dropped $2.50 a barrel or more than 10 percent in the past seven sessions, and traded Monday at $22.46 a barrel.

"I don't think we are going to break last year's levels in gasoline. I think we may not even get to 75.00 cents since crude has seen its highs," said Thomas Blakeslee, an analyst with Cargill Investor Services.
"I think this year we may get a rally to maybe 71.00 cents," said Jeff Foose, trader with KCS Energy in New Jersey.
On Monday, unleaded gasoline for March delivery rose 0.47 cent to 63.53 cents a gallon on the NYMEX.
"We are sort of neutral on gasoline for now," said Todd Miller, vice president and refined products trader at Morgan Stanley in New York.

According to the American Petroleum Institute, a trade group, gasoline inventories as of Jan. 31 were 7.4 million barrels below a year ago, while at this time in 1996, the year-over-year deficit was 6.3 million barrels.

But, rapid refining of readily available crude oil is expected to swiftly replenish stocks this year, with Iraqi oil flowing for the first time in more than six years. Also, boatloads of gasoline are arriving from Europe due to favourable prices.
Indeed, some traders were expecting gasoline imports to approach a historically high 650,000 barrels per day in February.
Even the AAA is encouraged by some easing in supply tightness, although it remains cautious overall.

"We continue to be concerned about tightness of gasoline supply, and we expect it to continue to exert upward pressure on spot prices," said Bill Jackman, AAA spokesman. "But, we are encouraged by gasoline stocks moving upward, and some analysts are even calling for a surplus by March," he said.

Last year's jump in gasoline prices was steepened by uncertainty over whether the U.N.-Iraq oil-for-food deal would be approved. But in December, the United Nations allowed Iraq to export oil in exchange for humanitarian aid for the first time since Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Iraqi supply has increased output of oil from members of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries to a 16-year high of 26.64 million barrels per day in January, according to a Reuters survey.

Meanwhile, dealers said talk that the current deficit of gasoline inventories could lead to a severe tightness come spring was simply alarmist. They said it echoed the concern of a heating oil shortage heard this past fall.

"We had the exact same talk coming into the winter about heating oil, but refiners have proven they can manage their inventories," said KCS Energy's Foose, adding, "We just don't have the same ingredients as last year. We are sucking up a lot of gasoline cargoes from everywhere it seems."
